units.translation: How this differs from μή [not] has been said above p. 171. The spelling of this particle is fourfold: οὐ before consonants, but never with aphaeresis, such as Seager introduced in Sophocles OR. 1526 when he conjectured οὐ ζήλου, which should have been said οὐκ ἐζήλου, and similar errors of others. οὐκ before vowels, but with a following rough breathing οὐχ. Where two syllables are needed, οὐχί is written. All these forms are not rarely joined with καί by crasis, κοὐ κοὐκ κοὐχ κουχί, (as Pr. 57 336 1069 1077 1080. Pers. 266 384 407 474. Ag. 30. Ch. 717 1021 1051. Eum. 121. Fr. 195, 6.) and in compounds with οὐ, such as κοὐδείς or by synizesis with ň, about which has been said above p. 147. Not rarely it is placed at the beginning of a question, as

many have discussed many things, of whom it will be enough to have mentioned Elmsley in his notes on Euripides Medea 1120 and Sophocles OC. 173, Hermann in his review of the Medea edited by Elmsley p. 389-391, and what has been collected in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 2345-7. But οὐ μή has an elliptical origin, said for οὐ δέος ἐστὶ μή [there is no fear that], as examples of the full expression teach, such as Herodotus 1, 84 οὐ γὰρ ἦν δεινὸν μὴ ἁλῷ κοτέ [for there was no danger that he would ever be caught], but often it is placed so that it is clear that writers have forgotten its origin. The construction of these particles is fourfold: with the subjunctive of the present of the verbs δύναμαι [I am able] and εἰμί [I am], with the subjunctive of any verbs of the first aorist, with the subjunctive of the second aorist, with the future indicative, and in indirect speech with the future optative: about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 363. As to the construction with the aorist, it is most usual for οὐ μή to be constructed with the subjunctive of the second aorist, rare with the subjunctive of the first aorist, and not admitted except in verbs which lack a second aorist.

About the particles μὴ οὐ we have spoken under μή p. 213, about οὐ μήν and οὐ μὴν — γε under μήν p. 216. The examples of Aeschylus pertain only to subjunctives of the aorist.
